title: Given an array sorted in non-decreasing order that may contain negative numbers, return a new array of the squares of each number, also sorted in non-decreasing order. Aim for linear time. (LeetCode: Squares of a Sorted Array)
shortTitle: Squaring a Sorted Array (Two Pointers from the Ends)
keyPoints: The largest squares hide at both ends of a sorted array because large negatives squared can exceed small positives squared.
Use two pointers at the ends, compare absolute values, square the bigger, and fill the result array from back to front.
Filling from the back produces a sorted array in a single linear pass without a separate sort step.
The naive approach of squaring everything then sorting costs O(n log n); the two-pointer method is O(n).
Compare absolute values rather than raw values because the sign does not matter for the square.
Cast to a wider type before multiplying to avoid integer overflow with large values.
If all elements are non-negative, a simple left-to-right pass preserves sorted order.

s1_definition.oneliner: The largest squares hide at the ends, so compare the two ends by magnitude, square the bigger, and fill the result from the back.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Problem** – given a sorted array with possible negatives, produce an array of squares also in sorted order.
- **Two-pointer approach** – place `left` at index 0 and `right` at the last index, and fill a result array from the back.
- **Comparison** – compare `Math.abs(arr[left])` with `Math.abs(arr[right])`; square whichever is larger and place it at the current back position.
- **Fill direction** – filling from the last index toward index zero builds the sorted output in one pass.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(n) space for the output array.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh at the National Bank of India has a sorted list of daily profit-and-loss figures where losses are negative and profits are positive. He needs the squared magnitudes sorted for a volatility measure. The biggest squared values live at the two ends of the sorted list. Priya reads from both ends inward, each time squaring whichever has the bigger magnitude and dropping it into the back of a new tray.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Squaring a sorted array that may contain negative numbers is trickier than it first looks, because a large negative value squared can be bigger than a small positive value squared. That means the largest squared values live at the two ends of the sorted array, and the smallest square is somewhere in the middle near the transition from negative to positive.

The efficient solution uses two pointers, one at each end of the input, and builds the result array from the back toward the front. At each step you compare the magnitudes of the two end values, square whichever is larger, place that square in the next slot from the back, and move that end's pointer inward. Because the largest remaining square is always at one of the two ends, filling the result from the last slot backward produces a fully sorted array in a single linear pass.

In Rajesh's work at the National Bank of India, the risk desk keeps daily profit-and-loss figures in a sorted array where losses are negative and profits are positive. The desk needs squared magnitudes sorted for a volatility measure, and with millions of figures across many books, squaring and re-sorting each time is too slow. The two-pointer linear method keeps the computation within the latency budget.

The senior-level details are about correctness and overflow. You compare magnitudes rather than raw values because the sign does not matter for the square, and you cast to a wider type before multiplying so that squaring large figures does not overflow. If the array has no negatives, squaring preserves order and a plain left-to-right pass works, but the moment negatives appear, the two-ended fill-from-the-back technique is the right tool.

Remember one sentence: compare magnitudes at both ends, square the bigger, and fill the result from back to front for O(n) sorted squares.
